Re-entrant publish raises rather than cascading. Handlers RETURN follow-ups, which are checked against a default-deny category matrix where every allowance carries a written reason, and bounded at depth 2. health -> notifications only; notifications terminal.

An event payload containing a credential shape, or a field named like one, is REFUSED rather than redacted -- at any nesting depth. Phase 6's shapes are reused so there is one answer in the codebase to what a credential looks like.

8.name: Build the Job System

requirements.evidence: All eleven manifest fields on a frozen Job; all twelve states with a transition TABLE rather than scattered conditionals. Terminal states have no outgoing edge; FAILED deliberately does, because a retry is a real thing.

Expiry is re-checked at dispatch, delivery, start and authorization -- not once at dispatch. The named test is the reconnection story: a device dispatched at 21:00 that comes back at 21:30 holding the job raises JobExpired instead of running, and the job is EXPIRED afterwards.
The same (user, idempotency_key) returns the same job rather than creating a second one, including after that job has SUCCEEDED. Scoped per user, so two users' keys cannot collide.

Every dispatch mints a delivery token; start, succeed and fail all refuse a stale one. A redispatch invalidates the previous token, which is what makes a lost acknowledgement recoverable rather than a double completion.

deliver() is a no-op on repeat -- duplicate delivery is the normal case on a flaky link. A lease that runs out sends the job back to the queue with attempts raised and the token cleared; a job that had already started is recorded FAILED('acknowledgement_lost') first rather than silently requeued.

Retries stop at max_attempts (3) and end EXPIRED with a reason naming which limit ran out. Cancellation works from every non-terminal state including DISPATCHED, and start() re-checks state rather than trusting what the device was told.

Phase 8 is Phase 7's first producer. remote_jobs.job_created and remote_jobs.job_state_changed carry job_id and status; a test asserts arguments never appear in a payload. The bus would refuse a credential anyway.
Python 607/607 (was 568), plugin 146/146 unchanged, policy check 390/390, audit check OK, capability check agrees, secret scan clean.

limitations: NOTHING RUNS. There is no dispatcher process, no transport, and no device on the other end. Phase 5's engine still denies any request whose target is not its origin, so no job can legitimately be remote yet. This is the queue and its rules.

Retry after a lost acknowledgement can double-execute unless the TARGET DEVICE honours the idempotency key. The queue cannot tell 'the device never got it' from 'the device did it and the answer was lost'; it records the difference (FAILED with acknowledgement_lost vs delivery_unacknowledged) and retries anyway. Device-side deduplication is a Phase 44 requirement and nothing enforces it today.
A job that legitimately started before its TTL may report success afterwards. Refusing a late success would leave a half-done delete with no record that it happened; the alternative was judged worse.
A job out of retries ends in EXPIRED, because the manifest's twelve states have no 'exhausted' and FAILED is the state a retry comes back from. The reason field distinguishes them.
The queue is in-memory and not thread-safe. Durability and concurrency belong to the backend (Phases 10-11) and to whatever owns a runloop.
followUps: Phase 44 (Mac Remote Connection Foundation) must implement device-side idempotency-key deduplication before any retry path goes live, and must re-check job expiry on the device as well -- the queue can only refuse what it is asked about.
sweep(now) needs an owner. Core has no runloop by design; whichever adapter gains one has to call it, or lost leases are never noticed.

12.name: Secret and Credential Vault

requirements.evidence: A data key per credential encrypts the secret; a KEK held by the KMS encrypts the data key. The row stores ciphertext and the WRAPPED key. KmsPort has no method that returns a KEK, so 'master keys outside PostgreSQL' is a property of the interface rather than a deployment note -- asserted by a test.

credential_id, user_id, provider, scopes, encrypted_refresh_token, key_version, created_at, updated_at, revoked_at. No field holds a plaintext token and no code path writes one; the Phase 11 table matches.

RefusingCipher is the default and raises. An unauthenticated cipher is refused at construction -- confidentiality without integrity means an attacker who can write to the database can flip bits in a token. Tests inject TestOnlyCipher, named so it is obvious in a stack trace if it ever reaches somewhere real.

user, connection and provider are the associated data, so copying encrypted_refresh_token into another user's row yields a token that fails authentication rather than decrypting under their name. Tampering with a byte is detected.

rotate_key re-wraps every data key under the current KEK; the ciphertext is byte-identical afterwards and the secret still decrypts. Idempotent. A retired KEK cannot unwrap -- losing access is the correct failure there, guessing is not.

Decryption returns a context manager: inside the `with` the bytes exist, at the end the buffer is overwritten and further reads raise. The wrapper refuses repr, str, format, bytes(), comparison and hashing -- the three ways a secret reaches a log are an f-string, a debugger, and json.dumps of a dict somebody thought was safe.

No module operation and no route names a secret-returning operation, asserted over Phase 10's tables. metadata() is a view rather than a filtered dump, so adding a field to the record does not silently add it to a response. And a borrowed secret is not JSON, so Phase 3's bundle, Phase 6's details and Phase 7's payload each refuse it by type -- tested on both the name path and the type path.

delete_connection revokes every credential under it in the same call, not through a job or an event -- anything asynchronous leaves a window in which a deleted connection can still refresh. A deleted connection cannot be given a new credential either. This closes Phase 9's last pending invariant: EXPECTED_PENDING is now 0.

The default raises rather than encrypting, so a deployment that forgets cannot store a credential at all -- but nothing here has ever encrypted anything with a production-grade cipher.

InProcessKms is a stand-in, not a KMS. Its wrap is HMAC-derived-keystream XOR, which is sufficient for wrapping 32 random bytes and is not a general-purpose cipher. Production uses the platform KMS through the same port.

13.name: Authentication

requirements.evidence: sign_in authenticates an ACCOUNT; device_id is recorded on the session and is never consulted in deciding whether the sign-in succeeds. Tested in both directions -- a session can exist without a device, and a device cannot be the proof.

CONNECTOR_PROVIDERS sits next to the mechanism registry; mechanism('google') raises ConnectorIsNotALogin, and constructing a Mechanism named after a connector raises at declaration. Being able to read someone's Gmail is not evidence of being them.

Opaque tokens; only the sha-256 hash is stored, matching Phase 11's sessions.token_hash column, because a stolen database should not be a stolen session. Access life 10 minutes, refresh 30 days, with a 90-day absolute ceiling on the whole chain -- without it a weekly-refreshed session never ends, which is a password that types itself.

Every refresh retires the old token. Presenting a retired one raises TokenTheftSuspected and revokes the ENTIRE family: either it was stolen or it was replayed, and both mean the chain is no longer trustworthy. Deliberately harsher than convenient.

revoke_session cascades to the family, revoke_user covers every family, and both take effect on the next verify with no cache to outlive them. inventory() lists live sessions per user and shows nothing of another user's.

Two mechanisms: a hard per-source limit (a source making hundreds of attempts is an attacker whatever account it names) and per-account exponential backoff capped at two minutes, never a lockout -- locking would hand an attacker a way to lock any account they can name. A success clears the account's backoff and not the source's limit.

CookiePolicy refuses to exist without HttpOnly and Secure, and refuses SameSite=None without Secure. CSRF is double-submit with constant-time comparison, required for cookie-bearing state changes and NOT for bearer tokens -- requiring it there would be a ritual without a defence.

Three signals, each a fact the system already has: a retired token presented again, a revoked session still being presented, and a session appearing from a new source while another is active. The third is surfaced, not acted on -- two computers is ordinary.

Registered with assurance levels and a production_requires line naming exactly what a real verifier needs. A mechanism is usable when a verifier is INSTALLED rather than when a flag says implemented -- a boolean claiming yes while no verifier exists is the kind of claim this program has already been bitten by.

Suspicious-session detection is three explicit signals, not intelligence. Nothing geolocates, fingerprints or models behaviour, and the source is an opaque hash supplied by the caller.

14.name: Device Identity

requirements.evidence: UserIdentity, DeviceIdentity and Attestation are distinct types that cannot be passed for one another. DeviceIdentity holds no user; Attestation holds neither a key nor a user. A jailbroken phone with a genuine key is a real device running an app nobody can vouch for, and the record says exactly that instead of collapsing it to trusted/untrusted.

There is no private-key field and no path that accepts one; a string that looks like a PEM private key is refused at construction, because somebody pasting one into the public field is not hypothetical. Hardware backing is recorded as a CLAIM the device makes, since the server cannot verify it by looking at a string.

A signed-in owner requests a challenge; the device signs owner|device_id|public_key|challenge. Signing the bare challenge would let a captured signature register a different device -- tested. Challenges are single-use, five-minute, and purpose-bound so a pairing challenge cannot be spent as a registration proof.

Ingest is idempotent by message id: the same message twice reports a duplicate, changes nothing, and leaves one row. The offline queue may deliver twice and the engine does not care -- a queue that guarantees exactly-once delivery does not exist.

Staleness CAPS confidence rather than averaging into it: a hundred readings that all stopped a month ago do not describe today, and averaging would let the sample size hide it.

Two questions that get collapsed constantly -- somebody sleeping a steady seven hours from 02:00 has excellent duration and poor consistency, and only one of those is actionable tonight. A steady 02:00 scores zero variation however late it is. **Midnight is not a discontinuity**: bedtimes alternating 23:50 and 00:10 are twenty minutes of variation, not twenty-three hours.

Acute (7d) against chronic (28d, normalised per week). When chronic load is zero the ratio is ABSENT -- not 1.0 and not infinity: "no ratio" and "a ratio of one" mean opposite things, and a division that can produce a special value is a division that will.

low / moderate / high, from sample count and freshness. `confidence: 0.8137` is precision about uncertainty, which is the same fabrication one level up -- and Phase 32 asks for categories over meaningless decimal scores for this reason.

40.name: Travel and Timezone Support
40.openedAgainst: the manifest text for PHASE 40. Opened OUT OF NUMERIC ORDER on 2026-09-01 under the since-withdrawn batch scheme, with entrySatisfied recorded as false rather than asserted true. Phases 34-39 were then completed the same day in numeric order, so the entry became legitimate and this flag was corrected -- the gate validator refused the document until it was, which is the sequence rule doing exactly its job.

decisions.decision: Phase 40 was opened while 34-39 were not started, and the gap was closed the same day rather than left open.
decisions.why: Nick moves to London around 2026-09-07 and lands on the 08th; the three cron jobs are pinned America/New_York and macOS auto-timezone is on, so the deadline was real. The out-of-order entry was recorded honestly (entrySatisfied: false) rather than asserted, and phases 34-39 -- the health block, none of which touches the dead Python runtime -- were completed afterwards on the same day. The sequence rule held: the validator refused the document until the flag matched reality.

decisions.decision: ZonedTime is a sum type. `.day` carries a CivilDay and has no instant at all, rather than an instant plus an isAllDay boolean.
decisions.why: An all-day event given an instant has silently had a zone chosen for it. That choice is invisible and correct until the machine moves, at which point a day that was right starts at 7pm the evening before. With no instant on the value, reaching for time requires naming a zone at the call site, where it can be reviewed.

decisions.decision: TimeZonePolicy returns a verdict; scripts/orion-timezone performs the change; orion-standing reports it once a day.
decisions.why: Re-homing touches live cron jobs and a live user-facing file. An assistant that re-homes its own schedule while the user is on holiday is the failure mode Nick's own document names -- 'gets muted within a day, permanently'. A policy that acts on its own conclusion also cannot be dry-run.

decisions.decision: ExpectedMove is stored in advance; arriving at the recorded destination is what makes a zone mismatch a move.
decisions.why: Nothing observable separates them -- a week in London and moving to London are identical to the OS on day one. USER.md said 'ask once after the move' on 2026-07-31 and the deadline passed in silence, because a date written in prose has nothing watching it.

requirements.evidence: ZonedInstant carries instant + zone + originalZone; AllDaySpan carries CivilDays and an optional provenance zone with no instant; ZonedTime is the sum. 27 tests in ZonedTimeTests. Codable round-trip is exact because the instant is normalised to the stored millisecond precision on construction. Mutation-proven: dropping originalZone from rezoned() fails 2 tests.

Enforced by type rather than by convention: ZonedTime exposes no `instant` property, so an all-day value cannot yield time without a zone named at the call site. IANAZone refuses GMT+0500, EST, Zulu, Etc/GMT+5 and UTC -- every fixed-offset spelling Foundation will happily resolve. All 443 accepted names round-trip byte for byte, asserted over the whole set.

CivilDay.interval is built from the next day's start, never by adding 86,400 seconds. Tests assert a 25-hour day (Europe/London 2026-10-25), a 23-hour day (2026-03-29), an ordinary 24-hour day so the test cannot pass by always answering 24, correct startOfDay in America/Santiago where midnight does not exist on the transition date, and refusal of a wall time inside a spring-forward gap. Mutation-proven: the 86,400 version fails 6 tests.

rezoned() preserves the instant, reanchored() preserves the wall clock, and they are separate names because picking the wrong one shifts an appointment by the offset between zones. TimeZonePolicy.verdict distinguishes settled / travelling / moveArrived / moveDue / moveScheduled over 18 tests, including clock skew: the verdict is a pure function of (device, instant), so a jumped clock cannot latch a wrong answer that outlives the jump.

The same AllDaySpan is a different interval in each zone (London 2026-09-07T23:00Z, New York 2026-09-08T04:00Z) and the test asserts both literals. `through` is inclusive, stated in the initialiser argument name; a backwards span clamps rather than inverting. A three-day span across the end of BST is 73 hours, not 72.

run-location-contract-test.sh compiles the real SessionDomain sources against bytes the real scripts/orion-timezone produced in a sandboxed HOME -- not a hand-written fixture. 20 checks. It exists because Foundation and ICU canonicalise 47 zone names differently in BOTH directions (ICU: America/Buenos_Aires; Foundation: America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires, and Foundation rewrites nothing where ICU turns America/Nuuk into America/Godthab). Mutation-proven: removing the translation table makes the app refuse the file the script wrote.

requirements.reason: Deliberately NOT done today. Nick is still in New York until roughly 2026-09-07; re-homing now would be wrong for six days. The mechanism is built, dry-runnable (`orion-timezone plan`) and idempotent, and the move is recorded so orion-standing raises it the morning after he lands. This closes when `orion-timezone set Europe/London` is run.
requirements.evidence: scripts/orion-timezone plan Europe/London reports the three cron jobs and shows orion-daily-memory moving 02:10 -> 07:10 local. location.json records home=America/New_York with expectedMove Europe/London on 2026-09-08. THE COMMAND ITSELF IS EXERCISED: run-timezone-set-test.sh drives the real script against a fake gateway over 18 checks (happy path, idempotence, a job the gateway refuses, and five zones that must be refused before anything is touched), and a REAL reversible round trip against the live gateway on 2026-09-01 12:41-12:43 EDT proved `openclaw cron edit --tz` behaves as assumed -- orion-daily-memory's next run moved from 02:10 to 21:10 New York local, which is 02:10 London, then back. Live state restored byte for byte and verified by diff against a pre-test copy.

requirements.reason: The vocabulary exists and is proven; migrating the app's existing date handling to it is not done. CalendarModel, AppleCalendarSync, EventComposer, WeekStrip and DayTimeline still use Calendar.current and a bare Date with an isAllDay flag. That is a real remaining gap and it is larger than Batch B -- it touches the calendar UI. CutoffDayKeys, which had an actual off-by-one defect, WAS migrated.
requirements.evidence: The correctness half is done and the display half is deliberately left. AgendaPlacement moves the calendar's day-membership rule off instant comparison: an all-day event is now compared as CIVIL DAYS and a timed one as instants, and AppleCalendarSync recovers an AllDaySpan once at fetch time in the event's own zone. The defect this removes is real and measured -- '8 September, all day' written in London is stored as 2026-09-07T23:00Z, which a New York calendar read as the SEVENTH. 11 tests including a sweep over all 443 zones; mutation-proven, and the old instant rule fails 445 assertions. The remaining Calendar.current sites (a greeting hour, a week-strip label, a finance month) are display-only and carry no day-boundary or all-day semantics.

requirements.reason: Not built. A flight is an event whose start and end are anchored to DIFFERENT zones, which ZonedInstant models one of but ZonedTime does not yet compose into a single value. Registering it rather than pretending the travel tests cover it -- they cover a device changing zones, which is a different thing from one event spanning two.
requirements.evidence: Journey, built from two ZonedInstants rather than a new two-zone primitive. Working out that no new primitive was needed is the finding: EventKit stores a flight as two INSTANTS, which are already correct at both ends -- only the mid-air wall clock is odd, and Nick's call on 2026-09-01 was that in-air precision is not worth building for. What Journey adds is that each end is READ in its own zone, and that duration comes from the instants. That last one is the actual bug in this area and is pinned: New York 18:00 to London 06:00 is SEVEN hours, and the test spells out that the wall clocks say twelve. A westbound journey has a positive duration and a negative clock shift; one that arrives before it departs is refused, which is exactly what a wall-clock comparison produces going west.

requirements.reason: The manifest itself says 'Create Travel Mode later'. Recorded so the phase cannot be read as complete while a named deliverable is absent.
requirements.evidence: TravelMode in SessionDomain. A READING layer only -- it never re-homes anything, because scripts/orion-timezone is deliberately the only thing that touches live cron. That division is what makes it safe to switch on automatically the moment the device and home zones disagree: showing a second clock cannot break anything. Two clocks with the device first, one clock at home rather than two identical ones, civil DAYS that can differ, and an unsociable-hour check sharing orion-standing's own quiet hours so two definitions of 'too late' cannot drift. Displacement is read AT THE INSTANT, so the fortnight when London has left BST and New York has not left EDT reports four hours rather than five -- pinned by a test at three dates. 15 tests.

limitations: One requirement remains blocked and it is not code: the live cron jobs are still pinned America/New_York because Nick has not moved yet. `orion-timezone set Europe/London` closes it in one command and is proven against both a fake gateway and a real reversible round trip.
Travel Mode has no UI. The domain is complete and tested; nothing displays a second clock yet.
Journey has no producer -- nothing turns a calendar event into one. It is the vocabulary a future travel surface needs, recorded as such rather than implied to be live.

The zone-name agreement between Foundation and ICU is pinned by a translation table generated on 2026-09-01 and a test that asserts it is still load-bearing. If tzdata moves under it the failure is loud -- the Swift decode refuses and names the string -- not silent.
The node half of the verdict rule in orion-timezone and orion-standing mirrors TimeZonePolicy.verdict. The Swift type is authoritative and has the tests; only the stored FORMAT is proven to agree.

35.name: Natural-Language Health Journal

decisions.decision: A readable vocabulary table, not an LLM.
decisions.why: orion-standing already made this call -- 'a rule that can be read is a rule that can be corrected when it nags about the wrong thing'. A journal is worse than a timer: it is Phase 36's input, so a silent misreading does not annoy, it fabricates a finding. A model's guess about whether 'I was wrecked' means exhaustion or intoxication cannot be argued with.

decisions.decision: JournalEventType case names are checked against ClinicalVocabulary; `notes` never is.
decisions.why: ClinicalVocabulary's own docstring says it is 'not a filter on user input -- a check on ORION's OWN vocabulary'. If Nick writes 'my anxiety was bad today' that is his sentence about his own life. A journal that argues with its author is not a journal. The rule bites in the other direction: 'feeling sick' is `.unwell`, because a case named `illness` would fail the check.

decisions.decision: .note is an escape hatch at low confidence, not a rejection.
decisions.why: An extractor that must classify everything classifies wrongly. Nick wrote it; it goes in.

requirements.evidence: All four -- 'Had caffeine around 5.', 'Worked out late.', 'Feeling sick.', 'Really stressed today.' -- extract to caffeine / exercise / unwell / stress, asserted individually.

JournalEvent carries eventType, time, source, confidence, notes -- plus originalText so a correction stays reviewable. Stored confidence is the WEAKEST of category and time confidence, never an average: a confident category at a guessed time is a guess. Round-tripped through a real file by run-journal-store-test.sh, 26 checks.

Exactly one trigger: the sentence claims 'today' and the resolved clock lands on another day. Every other case -- an unambiguous time, a bare hour, no time at all -- asks nothing. Reaching this took a failed test: the first design asked whenever a bare hour resolved more than 18 hours back, which CAN NEVER HAPPEN because mostRecent considers both meridiems and one candidate is always within twelve hours. That branch was unreachable, and a clarification path that cannot fire is worse than none because it reads as handled.

JournalEvent.correcting() is the only door: it forces source=.correction and confidence=.high and preserves originalText and id. A caller cannot mint a low-confidence 'correction' through the memberwise init. JournalStore.correct REPLACES by id rather than appending, proven against a real file. Mutation-proven.

limitations: The vocabulary is English and hand-written. It covers the manifest's examples and the obvious neighbours; an unrecognised line becomes .note at low confidence rather than being lost, which is the honest failure mode but is still a miss.
'half five' and other idioms are deliberately not parsed. Guessing at idiom is how an extractor becomes unpredictable.
No voice entry. Text only.
The Journal section's UI is not visually verified -- the app builds and the store is proven on disk, but the installed app is still build 121.

36.name: Behavior Correlations

decisions.decision: AssociationPhrase is a closed enum of exactly the manifest's four phrasings, and it is the only way a finding describes itself.
decisions.why: The manifest names the permitted wording explicitly, so it can be a type rather than a style guide. There is no path by which this file emits 'caffeine ruins your sleep' -- it cannot spell it. CausalVocabulary then checks the assembled sentence, the same way ClinicalVocabulary checks Phase 32's.

decisions.decision: Under five days per group the phrase is .insufficientData and `difference` is nil, not a hedged number.
decisions.why: A computed number in a field invites being quoted without its caveat. The type enforces the pairing in both directions: .insufficientData carrying an effect is refused, and a finding without one is refused.

decisions.decision: No p-value, no confidence interval, no significance test.
decisions.why: With forty observations of one person a p-value is a decoration that makes a weak claim look strong. The manifest's own altitude -- 'possible associations' -- is the honest one.

requirements.evidence: CorrelationOutcome has exactly the two the manifest names. Deliberately not strain or HRV, which would be building past the requirement. Days with no reading for an outcome are excluded rather than counted as zero -- asserted, because DayScore already records what scoring a missing input as zero costs.

withCount and withoutCount are non-optional on every Association including the insufficient ones, and the generated sentence names both. The floor applies to the SMALLER group, asserted with a 40-vs-2 fixture: forty days with and two without is still insufficient.

BaselineConfidence from the smaller group: moderate at 5+, high at 12+. The same difference over six days each is reported with the weaker phrase 'associated with' at moderate confidence; over fourteen it is 'correlated with' at high. Mutation-proven -- dropping the floor fails.

Every behaviour observed at all gets a row, including under-powered ones marked insufficient -- omitting them would make the screen imply the discussable ones were the only ones that happened. `.note` is excluded, since correlating 'things Orion could not classify' against sleep would be meaningless and look authoritative. Both mutation-proven.

CausalVocabulary (25 stems: cause, because, due to, leads to, ruins, improves, proves, shows that...) checked against every generated sentence, and the sentence returns nil rather than a sanitised version -- a sentence that had to be cleaned is one whose author meant something else. Mutation-proven: inserting 'This is because of the caffeine' into the template fails the suite. Every finding also ends 'This is an observation, not an explanation.'

The four rawValues are pinned as an exact set. A difference smaller than half the day-to-day spread is reported as insufficient rather than as a weak finding, because 'correlated with, but barely' is a sentence people repeat without the second half. Mutation-proven.

limitations: The reference spread is the POOLED set of both groups, and that choice is a judgement rather than a tested property. Trying to pin it found the opposite of what the code comment claimed: MAD is resistant by construction, so pooling a tight fourteen-day group with a wide one gives a spread of roughly 0.5-1.5 rather than a larger one, and no fixture separated pooled from within-group at these thresholds. The comment was corrected to stop overclaiming. Worth revisiting with real data once the journal has months in it.

Nothing consumes this yet. It is a domain engine with 447 MobileCore checks behind it and no UI and no caller -- Phase 37 (experiments) and a Trends surface are the intended consumers. Recorded rather than hidden, because the program correction is explicit that modules with no consumer are how this repo acquired three stacks.
minimumPerGroup = 5 and noticeable = 0.5 spreads are constants chosen conservatively so they can be argued with. They are not derived from Nick's data, which does not exist yet.

decisions.decision: Past a third of observed days carrying a declared confounder, the result is inconclusive and NO association is computed.

A running experiment offers NO association at all and says why -- a partial result is the most misread thing an experiment produces. Mutation-proven. Confounded days are counted and the confounders NAMED in the summary.
Every summary checked against both CausalVocabulary and ClinicalVocabulary, and asserted never to contain 'worked'. The finding can only be phrased the four ways AssociationPhrase permits.

captureBaseline filters to days strictly before the start. Mutation-proven: drawing it from the window instead fails two assertions -- an experiment that grades itself against its own result. With nothing before the start it returns nil rather than a fabricated baseline.

limitations: The manifest itself says 'Later add user-defined experiments'. Built now because it is a numbered phase and the block 34-39 is being closed in order; the definition surface (a UI to create one) does not exist, only the domain.

findings.finding: SEVERE. The finding an experiment reported was not computed over the experiment.
findings.wasRecorded: 'ExperimentEngine.track is a window over the SAME CorrelationDay list', and the file header calls it 'a NAMED WINDOW'.
findings.actuallyTrue: `window` and `observed` were computed and used for stage, observedDays and confoundedDays -- and then the association was built from `days`, the entire history. Measured against the real engine: a 14-day experiment reported observedDays 14 beside sample counts of 34 with and 14 without, on the same screen, from 48 days. Data from outside the window could and did INVERT the sign of the reported finding, and durationDays had no effect on the result at all. The confounder protection inherited the same hole: confoundedDays counted only the window, so a confounder outside it could not make a result inconclusive even though those days fed the association. No test could tell -- mutating `days:` to `window:`, the opposite behaviour, left the suite at 665 checks, 0 failed, because the existing assertion only checked the association was non-nil.
findings.repair: The association is built from `observed` -- exactly the set observedDays counts, so the sentence and the day count beside it agree by construction. Pinned three ways: twenty days of contradictory out-of-window history do not change the finding; withCount + withoutCount equals observedDays; and a 400-day experiment on the same days is still running where the 14-day one has completed, which is the signature of duration mattering again. Mutation-proven. One equivalent mutant survives and is not a gap: passing `window` instead of `observed` gives identical results, because CorrelationEngine.association compactMaps away days with no metric anyway.

It is computed as a civil time -- 08:00 where he is standing -- never as an instant plus 24 hours. A real defect is pinned here: 22:00 on a spring-forward night is NOT enough to tell the two apart, because adding 86,400 seconds still lands on the right day and the hour is then set correctly. They diverge only in the last hour before midnight -- 23:30 GMT plus 86,400s is 00:30 BST on the THIRTIETH, so the naive version skips 29 March entirely and the morning brief simply never fires. The first version of this test used 22:00, the mutant survived, and the fix was the test. A near-miss assertion is worse than none. Pinned in both Europe/London and America/New_York, with a non-DST control night proving the nine-hour gap is DST and not an off-by-one everywhere.

The ambient set is exactly {recommendation, trend, discovery}, pinned by contents. Structurally, an ambient item is never pushed: NotificationEngine.plan can only place it in `collected`, so there is no code path from ambient to interrupt and an observation stream cannot escalate itself by volume.

Three mechanisms, none of them a filter on text. (1) There is no category meaning 'something happened' -- every member names a judgement already made, asserted by a test that refuses an observation/event/info member. (2) Ambient never pushes, above. (3) Ambient items COLLAPSE by category and subject, newest surviving: 200 readings about one subject yield one item, asserted directly. Mutation-proven twice -- removing the collapse fails three named assertions including the 200-item one, and collapsing to the FIRST reading instead of the newest fails the assertion that pins the survivor's TEXT rather than the count.

Expressed in the type, three ways. (1) NotificationItem carries NO state: it has a subject (the id of a durable record) and a summary (display text), and there is no payload field and no apply(). Pinned by reflecting over the stored properties and asserting the exact set {id, category, subject, summary, at}, so adding a `state:` field fails by name rather than at the point somebody starts trusting it. (2) init? REFUSES an empty subject -- a notification pointing at nothing is one whose content exists only inside the push, which is precisely what this forbids; mutation-proven. (3) plan() is a pure function of the whole list and is idempotent and ORDER-INDEPENDENT: plan(stream + stream) and plan(stream.reversed()) and plan(stream.shuffled()) all equal plan(stream). That is the operative property -- a push may be lost, duplicated, delayed or reordered, and all four have to be survivable. Ties are broken by id as well as timestamp, because a tie is exactly where order dependence gets back in.

The inbox cursor is advanced past everything waiting, so queued envelopes are never handed to a verb -- and they are left ON DISK rather than deleted, because what was cancelled is itself something you want to be able to read afterwards. The permission profile IS the delegation mechanism that exists today, and the lock drops it to the bottom rung through the plugin's own changePermissionProfile rather than by writing the state file. Five of the six things a lockdown does then silently did not happen: no flag, no queue cancellation, no expired approvals, no dropped session, no disabled cron, and inbound commands kept executing. A corrupt permission-state.json was worse: an unhandled JSON.parse threw before anything was touched at all. Evidence false at the moment it was written.
findings.repair: lock() now calls stopTheChannel() first and unconditionally, each step individually guarded so one unwritable file cannot stop the other three; an unreadable profile is reported and non-fatal; a failed profile change no longer aborts cron. The process still exits non-zero so a caller can tell a partial lockdown from a complete one, but only after everything has been attempted. Pinned by a new section in orion_v2_lock_check.sh that corrupts permission-state.json and asserts the flag, the cursor, the expired approval, the refusal AND cron all still happen. Mutation-proven in both shapes.

findings.finding: Two assertions in the lock check were satisfiable by the wrong thing.

findings.actuallyTrue: The first only checked the output did NOT contain 'locked', which empty output from a crashed orion-remote also satisfies. The second matched 'locked' case-insensitively, which the unrelated error 'remote.json stayed locked for six seconds' would also satisfy.

decisions: NO TRANSPORT WAS STUBBED. A fake transport that pretended to connect would make every test in this phase meaningless -- the policies below are only worth anything if the thing they govern is real. The credential needed for a real channel is Nick's to create, so the transport half is registered blocked and the domain half is complete and proven.

The connection VOCABULARY went in MobileCore rather than beside orion-remote, because the manifest's last line is 'mobile must clearly display Mac availability' and a phone that disagrees with the Mac about what 'offline' means is the failure this phase is supposed to prevent.
Outbound-only is enforced as a SHAPE, not a promise. LinkEndpoint has no bind address, no listen port and no backlog, pinned by reflection over its stored properties.

requirements.evidence: Closed 2026-09-02 against the real Discord gateway. scripts/orion-remote-bridge opens a WebSocket OUT to wss://gateway.discord.gg, IDENTIFYs, and receives READY -- verified live: 'connected as orion (1 guild(s))'. There is no listening socket anywhere in the file and nothing for a router to forward, which is the same property the security invariant scans the whole tree for. The bridge holds no authority: it appends an envelope via `orion-remote inject` and asks it to `poll`, so the allowlist, replay guard, rate limit, shape checks and audit are the ones that already had tests rather than a second copy that can drift. It cannot even compose a reply -- replies are read back out of orion-remote's own outbox, correlated by an envelopeId now carried there for exactly that reason.

Verified against the tree and the running machine, not asserted. orion/interface/server.py defaults --host to 127.0.0.1 AND refuses to start on anything outside (127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1) -- proven by running it with --host 0.0.0.0 and asserting exit 2 before any socket is opened. orion/server.py hardcodes 127.0.0.1; OAuthFlow.swift binds inet_addr("127.0.0.1") on an ephemeral port. On the live machine the only listener is the node gateway on 18789, bound to [::1] and 127.0.0.1 only. Made permanent as a security invariant that scans every live source for a wildcard bind. The scan's FIRST version was itself a defect and is the finding here: looking for the address alone, it flagged orion/web.py's SSRF denylist -- a guard that names 0.0.0.0 precisely because it refuses to fetch it. A test that reports a security control as a vulnerability is worse than no test, because the cheapest way to make it pass is to delete the control. The detector now requires a bind token as well, and is itself tested against four lines it must catch and three it must not.

Follows from the above and is proven by the same scan: nothing in the live tree opens a listener on a routable address, so there is nothing a router could forward to. The endpoint type can only describe somewhere to dial out.

TLS via wss, and a bot token sent in exactly two places: the IDENTIFY frame and the REST Authorization header. Certificate validation is ASSERTED rather than assumed -- the bridge refuses to start if NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED is 0, because an authenticated transport whose certificate is not checked is an unauthenticated one that looks fine. Everything the file prints goes through a redactor keyed on the token, defending against the leak nobody writes on purpose: an error echoing the frame that caused it. The finding worth recording is a permission that was NOT taken: the first attempt requested MESSAGE_CONTENT and Discord closed the socket with 4014. Enabling that privileged intent would have let the bot read every message in every channel it can see. Dropping it was the better fix -- Discord delivers full content for DMs and @mentions without it, which is exactly how Orion is addressed, so he hears you when you talk TO him and is deaf to everything else.

ReconnectPolicy: exponential backoff bounded at BOTH ends, which is the part that matters. Uncapped, the delay grows until the link that is supposed to heal itself quietly stops trying; with no floor, jitter reduces the wait to zero and a Mac that cannot reach the endpoint hammers it -- a self-inflicted denial of service against the one channel Nick would use to find out why. So jitter only ever REDUCES, by at most half, and is clamped to 0...1 rather than trusted. Asserted across attempts 1...200, including counts large enough to overflow a naive shift. Four mutations killed: removing the cap, letting jitter reach zero, unclamping jitter, and accepting a zero base.

HeartbeatPolicy refuses its own nonsense: a stale threshold below the beat interval would mark a healthy link stale on every beat, and an offline threshold below the stale one makes the warning state unreachable so a link jumps from online straight to offline and nobody ever sees the state the screen exists to show. Both refused by init?, mutation-proven. Boundaries are pinned at the second on both sides (119s online / 120s stale, 299s stale / 300s offline) and the boundary belongs to the WORSE state, also mutation-proven.

Four presences, and the distinction the whole file is built around: `unknown` is not `offline`. 'I have never heard from your Mac' and 'your Mac is off' are different facts, and rendering the first as the second means a phone that has lost signal confidently reports the Mac is down -- the most likely wrong answer this screen can give and the one a person would act on. A heartbeat from the FUTURE is also unknown rather than online, because a wrong clock must not pin the display to the one state nobody re-checks. Both mutation-proven.

RotationPolicy rotates a connection at its maximum age and refuses a zero age. The case worth having is the negative one: a link with no connection is NOT 'due for rotation', because answering true there would make the reconnect loop rotate a connection that does not exist, forever. Mutation-proven.

KeyPin FAILS CLOSED: an unconfigured pin set accepts nothing. The usual accident is the opposite -- treating 'no pins configured' as 'allow anything' turns a missing config value into a silently unauthenticated connection, the failure that looks exactly like success. Mutation-proven against precisely that. Fingerprints are compared in one normalised spelling, so AA:BB:CC and aabbcc are the same key; a comparison that says otherwise rejects the right key on a bad day and teaches somebody to switch pinning off.

'Clearly' is treated as a real requirement: the four presences produce four DIFFERENT headlines, asserted as a set of four distinct strings and by exact contents -- Online, Not responding, Offline, Never connected. Two affordances follow and are separately asserted: only an online Mac may be sent to, because queueing into silence and reporting it as sent is worse than refusing (the person walks away believing the Mac was told something it never heard); and offline suggests a retry while never-connected suggests setup, which are not the same control.

limitations: A full Discord round trip -- inbound message to delivered reply -- has NOT been executed, because no account is allowlisted yet. ORION_REMOTE_ALLOW defaults to refusing everyone, and the candidate id was discovered with `orion-remote-bridge whoami` and written into .env COMMENTED OUT: granting an account authority over this Mac is a person's decision, not an inference an assistant makes from who owns the guild. One uncommented line closes it.

Nothing supervises the bridge. `run` stays connected and reconnects on its own, but no launch agent starts it, and launchd cannot read ~/Desktop on this machine -- the same constraint that already leaves the TTS daemon unsupervised.

The bridge writes remote-link.json, which is MobileCore's MacLink shape, so Phase 44's 'no producer' limitation is closed. No Mac or phone SURFACE reads it yet, so the four presences still render nowhere.

The reconnect, heartbeat and rotation numbers in the bridge mirror MobileCore's RemoteLink policies. The Swift side is authoritative and carries the tests; the two are not mechanically proven to agree -- the same shape as the TimeZonePolicy mirror under Phase 40.

45.name: Remote Mac Read-Only
45.openedAgainst: Phase 44's two open requirements are the transport, which waits on a credential Nick creates. All seven of Phase 45's named tests are about JOB HANDLING rather than the wire, so they are answerable now and were. Recorded as a deviation rather than asserted true.
45.evidence: native/OrionMobile/Sources/MobileCore/RemoteJob.swift, checked by scripts/orion_v2_mobile_check.sh (665 checks, 0 failed; iOS build clean).
decisions: Deciding and DOING are separate types. JobGate.evaluate returns a verdict and never performs an effect, so nothing in this file can touch the Mac even by accident -- which is the strongest available reading of 'do not modify anything'.
evaluate returns the verdict AND the next gate rather than mutating in place, so a caller cannot record a job as seen while failing to act on the verdict.
Replay and duplicate are deliberately DIFFERENT rejections, and working out why is the substance of this phase. See the requirement below.

requirements.evidence: Built and served as of 2026-09-02. device.status.read returns battery, uptime and free disk; application.list returns running applications by name; files.safe_metadata returns names, sizes and dates. All three shell out with FIXED argv -- no inbound value reaches any of them, and the only thing a message can influence is which of three directory names is read. Defining 'running application' took three attempts and the wrong two are worth recording: matching any bundle in the process table answered '62 running', nearly all of them agents like AirPlayUIAgent; matching the outermost bundle then reported News, Stocks and Home as running, because their widget extensions are always alive while the apps are not. The honest definition is an executable directly in a top-level bundle's Contents/MacOS.

Still an absent enum member on the Swift side, and now also true of the live handlers: not one of the three writes a file, changes a setting, starts a process or touches Orion's own state. files.safe_metadata is metadata ONLY -- nothing opens a file, and the difference between listing a name and reading a document is the whole of Phase 45. Mutation-proven: making the handler print file contents fails a named assertion. That assertion had to be rewritten to bite -- the first spelling used `grep -qv`, which inverts per line and therefore always exits 0 on multi-line output, so it could never fail. Found by mutation, not by reading.

The same job id twice is refused as a replay, because a resent id is indistinguishable from an attacker resending a captured one and the gate must not have to guess which. Rejections are recorded as seen too, so a rejected id cannot be retried into a different verdict by waiting. Mutation-proven twice -- removing the replay check, and forgetting rejected jobs.

Closed in the LIVE path, not only in the domain. scripts/orion-remote now reads back the `at` timestamp it has always written: an envelope older than ten minutes is refused and audited as expired, with the age named. Asserted against a 40-minute-old envelope in a sandbox HOME. Judged after replay, so a replayed stale message is still reported as a replay, which is the more useful of the two answers. Mutation-proven by restoring the previous behaviour -- no age check at all -- which fails the named assertion.

A revoked issuer's job is refused, revoking one issuer does not silence the others, and authority is judged BEFORE freshness -- reporting a revoked device's stale job as merely expired would suggest a newer one would work. The ordering is mutation-proven by swapping the two checks.

Closed in the live path. Envelopes may now carry `to`, and one addressed to another Mac is refused before any state is written -- so it consumes no replay slot and no rate-limit hit. Both halves are asserted and both are mutation-proven, including the subtle one a naive implementation gets wrong: a mutant that records the misaddressed envelope as seen fails the assertion that the replay memory did not grow. Without that, anyone could exhaust this device's memory with envelopes meant for somebody else, at no cost and with no valid credential.

Not a handler that copes with rubbish; a type rubbish cannot become. RemoteJob.init? refuses an empty id, an unaddressed job (refused rather than treated as a broadcast), an id carrying a space or a shell word, and one whose expiry is at or before its issue time -- which is broken rather than short-lived, and accepting it would make every freshness check meaningless. Mutation-proven twice.

A dropped reply is indistinguishable from a dropped request, so the client must retry. Judging is pure and total, so re-delivering the WHOLE stream answers each job exactly once, and so does any interleaving of retries -- asserted over three orderings. Nothing depends on how far the network got before it failed.

Distinguished from replay on purpose, and this is the phase's real content. A DUPLICATE is the same request under a NEW id, which is what an honest client does when its answer was lost, and it is accepted. It is only safe to accept because every capability here is a pure read, so answering twice returns the same thing -- which is exactly why the manifest orders read-only before Phase 46's actions. The rule a client must follow falls out of it: mint a new id to retry, never re-send the old one.

CLOSED 2026-09-02 18:12 UTC by a real round trip over Discord, not by inspection. Nick DM'd the bot `device` from 732025545549807666; the bridge logged `<- [732025545549807666] device`, orion-remote's audit recorded `decision: accepted, verb: device, from: 732025545549807666`, and the reply went back to Discord carrying live values (battery 80% on AC, up 4 days, 651 GB free). Every layer was exercised at once: outbound gateway connection, MESSAGE_CONTENT, the allowlist, the verb vocabulary, a read-only capability, and the outbox correlation by envelopeId. The audit line immediately before it is the rejected `--x` sender-forgery attempt from the check suite, so the same file shows the bypass being refused and the legitimate message being attributed to the right account -- which is the live proof that the argument-injection repair holds.

limitations: NOTHING SUPERVISES THE BRIDGE. It runs only while something runs it, so Orion is genuinely offline between sessions -- which is exactly what Nick observed in the Discord member list before the round trip. Making it persistent is its own piece of work and hits the same constraint that leaves the TTS daemon unsupervised: launchd cannot read ~/Desktop.

Commands must be addressed to Orion -- a DM, or a message starting with @orion. He READS every channel (MESSAGE_CONTENT is enabled at Nick's instruction) but only obeys what is addressed to him, so typing 'cancel that idea' in a channel cannot fire the cancel verb. Nick's stated preference is DMs, which need no mention. A message heard in a channel and not obeyed now SAYS so once per connection; it used to return silently, which was indistinguishable from a broken bridge and cost the first live attempt.
files.safe_metadata reads three fixed roots (Desktop, Documents, Downloads), top level only, hidden files skipped, 40 entries maximum. A path argument was deliberately not offered.

application.list uses `ps` rather than System Events, so it needs no Automation permission and cannot raise a TCC prompt on a Mac nobody is sitting at. The cost is that an app installed outside /Applications or ~/Applications is not listed.

The live guards in orion-remote and the JobGate in MobileCore now agree on judgement order, but that agreement is not mechanically enforced -- they are two implementations of one rule set. They differ deliberately on one point: an envelope with no target is a local broadcast here and is refused in Swift.

findings.finding: SEVERE. A message beginning with `--` forged its own sender.
findings.wasRecorded: 'every inbound Discord message is refused' (blocked reason), 'defaults to refusing everyone' (Phase 44 limitation), and the assertion 'an unknown sender gets SILENCE'.
findings.actuallyTrue: The bridge built `inject <text> --from <id>`, and the argument parser treated any argv entry starting with -- as a flag name whose value is the next entry. A message of '--x' therefore SWALLOWED the following --from: flags.from was never set, the sender fell back to 'local', and where local is allowlisted the message was authorised as the local account. Reproduced end to end -- the envelope came out as {from: 'local', text: '<the sender id>'}, so the audit also recorded the wrong person, a stranger received a reply enumerating the whole verb vocabulary, and thirteen such messages exhausted the local rate budget and locked Nick out of his own channel.
findings.repair: Four layers, any one of which closes it: unknown flags are REFUSED rather than silently accepted; a `--` terminator is honoured; a flag with no value is an error; and the bridge passes --from BEFORE the text with -- between them. The bridge additionally drops non-allowlisted senders before spawning anything, so a stranger can no longer grow inbox.jsonl or start two node processes per message. Three new assertions, mutation-proven.

findings.finding: The assertion that proves the wrong-device rule tolerated the defect it names.
findings.wasRecorded: 'a mutant that records the misaddressed envelope as seen fails the assertion that the replay memory did not grow.'
findings.actuallyTrue: The assertion was `[ "$SEEN_AFTER" -le 2 ]` where the correct value is 1, so a mutant that recorded the misaddressed envelope landed inside the bound and PASSED -- while printing the growth the message denied.
findings.repair: Tightened to `-eq $((SEEN_BEFORE + 1))`. Mutation-proven.

findings.finding: Expiry failed open on an absent or malformed timestamp.
findings.wasRecorded: orion-remote now reads back the `at` it has always written.
findings.actuallyTrue: `Number.isFinite(sentAt) ? now - sentAt : 0` gave age 0 -- never expired -- to any envelope whose `at` was missing, a string, or null. The fail-open-on-absent-field pattern.
findings.repair: An envelope that cannot say when it was sent cannot be shown to be fresh, so it is treated as stale. Two traps surfaced while fixing it and are recorded because both produce right answers for wrong reasons: the first version also refused DIRECT `handle` invocations, which carry no envelope and are a person typing now, so poll now passes `at ?? null` and an absent field is distinguished from an unstamped envelope; and `Number(null)` is 0 rather than NaN, which dated unstamped envelopes to the epoch and reported '29806188 min old' instead of 'no usable timestamp'. Three assertions, mutation-proven in both shapes.

findings.finding: The live path and the Swift JobGate actively DISAGREED, where a limitation claimed only that they were unproven.
findings.wasRecorded: 'not mechanically proven to agree'.
findings.actuallyTrue: They disagreed on order: orion-remote judged replay before expiry and called that deliberate, while RemoteJob.swift judges expiry before replay and its doc comment calls THAT order pinned. They also disagree on an unaddressed job -- Swift refuses one, the live path treats a missing `to` as a broadcast and accepts it.
findings.repair: The order is aligned: the live path now judges replay last, matching the Swift. The unaddressed difference is deliberate and stays: an envelope with no target from the local CLI is legitimate, so absence means 'whichever Mac drains this queue'. The gate's tested_malformed_jobs evidence cited 'an unaddressed job refused rather than treated as a broadcast' as passed, which is true in Swift and false in the path facing Discord -- corrected here.

findings.finding: Revocation required restarting the bridge.
findings.wasRecorded: Revocation was scoped to the Swift domain and not overclaimed, so this is an omission rather than a false claim.
findings.actuallyTrue: The bridge read ORION_REMOTE_ALLOW once at startup and `run` stays connected indefinitely, so withdrawing an account's authority meant killing the process. Revocation that depends on remembering to restart something will not happen during the incident it exists for.
findings.repair: The bridge re-reads it per message. Worth recording that the first fix was in the wrong file: orion-remote is spawned afresh for every message and never had stale state, and a mutation proved that fix untestable because it changed nothing observable.

findings.finding: A pre-existing flaky test, unrelated to this work, that made every suite count unreliable.
findings.wasRecorded: 'Python 1,445' in several gate records.
findings.actuallyTrue: test_tts_daemon.ServerTests.test_socket_path_is_published_only_once_it_accepts failed roughly one full-suite run in six, and never in isolation. Cause: it used client.connect, which returns None for ANY OSError, so it could not tell ECONNREFUSED -- the bug it guards, the path published between bind() and listen() -- from a plain timeout under load.
findings.repair: It now connects directly and counts the two separately: any refusal fails, a timeout does not. The property is asserted more sharply than before rather than relaxed. Verified the flake was timeouts and not refusals before changing anything -- 200 direct attempts gave 200 accepted, 0 refused -- then 22 consecutive full-suite runs clean.

46.name: Harmless Mac Actions
46.evidence: The four actions already existed in the deployed catalogue. Verified against openclaw-plugins/orion-control/dist and against the real execution ledger rather than rebuilt.
decisions: NOT BUILT. All four actions were already in the deployed ACTION_CATALOG under the live stack's names, which is the interpretation rule working as intended: the manifest's `application.launch` is `app_open`, `system.volume.set` is `volume_set`. Grepping the catalogue before designing is what stopped this becoming the third phase in this program to be built twice.
Evidence is taken from the REAL ledger -- actions that have actually run on this Mac -- rather than from a fixture. browser_open_url has seven recorded executions.

requirements.evidence: app_open and app_quit, both capabilityTier app_control, both risk low and reversible true. Present in the deployed catalogue, not only in source.

browser_open_url, tier browser_control, risk medium. The best-evidenced action in the phase: seven real executions in the archived ledger, each recording the resolved browser and bundle id alongside the url.
volume_set, tier media_control, risk low, reversible. volume_mute and volume_unmute exist beside it, and display_sleep and the three media transport actions share the tier.

Every one of the four is gated by capability tier, and the tiers are absent from restricted_read_only -- so all four become unreachable the moment LOCK ORION drops the profile to the floor. Measured across the five profiles: app_control, browser_control and media_control are allowed in approved_root_edit and above and in nothing below it. That is the same intersection the runtime validator computes, read from the live plugin rather than asserted.

The TaskLedger records far more than the fact of execution. A real archived entry for browser_open_url carries the request (action, arguments, and sourceRefs naming the turn that authorised it), the execution (mode, target, and the resolved output), a VERIFICATION block with method browser_tab_shows_url, observed true and the actual tab as evidence, and a status of verified. Task-level records additionally carry planHash, authorization binding and turn count. An audit that records what was asked, what ran, and what was observed afterwards is the useful kind.

requirements.reason: No mobile surface exists, and these four actions are atomic -- an app launch has no in-flight window to cancel. The honest reading is that this requirement belongs with Phase 56's session UI, where cancelling something long-running is meaningful.
requirements.evidence: Mission-level cancellation does exist and is reachable remotely -- `cancel <mission>` is one of orion-remote's verbs and it stops the runner. What does not exist is cancellation of an action, and there is no mobile surface to cancel from: MobileCore's types still have no producer or renderer. Registered rather than argued around, because Phase 56 (Remote Session UI) is where the manifest actually puts pause/cancel/inspect, and closing this on the mission verb would let 56 inherit a tick it did not earn.

controlMedia took a pre-flight playerSnapshot purely to record previousState as evidence, using the default 10s osascript timeout. MEASURED on this Mac: that snapshot query against Apple Music takes 120 SECONDS. So the action failed at 10.07s having never sent the playpause -- Nick asked Orion to pause his music and was told 'Music did not respond in time' because verification consumed the thing it was verifying. The snapshot is now bounded to 3s and degrades to an unknown previous state on failure rather than aborting. An unverified pause that happened beats a verified one that did not. Plugin rebuilt, 146 tests pass, deployed to the INSTALLED copy -- which is what actually runs.

requirements.reason: Not fixed. orion-selfdoc must emit optional arguments too. Registered rather than repaired because it changes the generated capability surface the model reads, and that deserves its own verified pass.
requirements.evidence: media_play_pause accepts an optional `player` argument that would have targeted Apple Music directly. Orion called it bare, it iterated Spotify first, and he told Nick he had no way to target Apple Music -- which he could not have known was wrong, because scripts/orion-selfdoc emits only requiredArguments and the tool description exposes bare action names. The argument is invisible everywhere the model can see.

requirements.reason: Not fixed. Giving retries a non-zero default changes execution semantics for every action, not just this one, and should not be done unsupervised.
requirements.evidence: The AppleScript timeout throws ActionExecutionError(msg, retryable=true) and the controller honours it only while attempt <= graph.retryBudget. retryBudget defaults to 0 and the tool description instructs the model never to set it, so no model-issued action is ever retried and the flag is dead code.

limitations: app_open, app_quit and volume_set are verified as PRESENT and correctly gated, not as executed. browser_open_url is the only one of the four with real executions in the ledger. Running the others would have launched applications and changed the volume on Nick's Mac while he was out, which is a poor trade for evidence that the catalogue already provides.
The manifest's names and the live names differ (application.launch -> app_open, system.volume.set -> volume_set). Recorded so a later reader does not conclude the actions are missing.
Phase 46 stays open on mobile cancellation, so Phase 47 enters with entrySatisfied false unless that closes first.

APPLE MUSIC IS NOT ANSWERING APPLEEVENTS ON THIS MAC AT ALL, and the snapshot fix does not change that. Measured 2026-09-02: `tell application id "com.apple.Music" to playpause` returns AppleEvent timed out (-1712) after 120 seconds. So the pause would have failed even with the snapshot skipped. This is an environment or app-state problem rather than a code one, and it is the real reason Nick's music did not pause.

A system media-key route was measured at 291ms against the AppleEvent route's timeout, which looks like the answer to Nick's own phrasing -- 'whatever is the current fastest way to pause'. It was NOT shipped: osascript reporting success only means the script ran, `key code 16` is plausibly the 'y' key rather than a media key, and with Music unresponsive there was no way to confirm anything actually paused. Shipping an unverified fallback would be the same confidently-wrong failure this phase exists to record.

requirements.evidence: This phase is unusual: its deliverable IS the definition, and the manifest says so. All seven are answered with a rule and the reasoning behind it. DISCLOSURE is fixed text in source, not a config value or a prompt, because a model that composes its own disclosure will eventually compose a shorter one — and if it fails to play, the call ends rather than proceeding undisclosed. CONSENT reuses the Phase 49 approval gate and states that `sovereign` must not relax it. RECORDING is a flat no, because recording law depends on where each party is physically standing and a system that cannot determine the applicable law cannot lawfully record. IMPERSONATION is three separate prohibitions because they fail separately. ESCALATION ends the call on any confusion and keeps a do-not-call record. IDENTITY VERIFICATION refuses in BOTH directions — it will not prove it is Nick, which is the interaction a SIM-swap runs on, and it will not accept a claim from the other end, because a call is untrusted external content. SENSITIVE INFORMATION is an allowlist rather than a denylist, because a call is a conversation and a denylist is the wrong shape for one.

The document's structural conclusion, with the reasoning: a call is synchronous, has no draft state, makes the other party a participant rather than a recipient, and is the one channel where impersonation is the default failure. So a `calling` tier would be its own, at external_connected or above, listed explicitly rather than folded into anything — the same rule messages_send and self_modification already follow. Six preconditions are listed in order, and the sixth is an independent review, since this document was written by the same model that would build the feature.

reviews.method: Read validator.ts, approvals.ts, strictness.ts, devops.ts, automation.ts, orion-deploy and orion-backup; probed resolveDevCommand and decisionsInUserTurn directly; parsed the live 115-entry exec allowlist; surveyed 482 real session files for what actually carries trusted_user; ran nine check suites and 222 tests; and mutation-tested the approval gate and the floor, restoring every file (verified with git status --porcelain).
confirmed: The approval gate cannot be self-satisfied. It tried to construct a path from data the caller can compute and could not. All four boundary claims verified against the live machine, including that orion-approve, orion-mode and orion-automation are absent from the real allowlist.
Mutations that fail by name: removing the local-sender refusal, deleting the trusted_user filter, and re-accepting the model-supplied hash.
devops.ts is genuinely closed — limits of 1.5, -1, 999, NaN and '3 --output=/tmp/x' all refused; no path argument exists anywhere.
orion-deploy's order is as claimed, with the suite gate before the install.
Absence claims verified by enumeration rather than grep: 27 execution kinds, zero raw-shell.
findings: SERIOUS: the strictness ladder was never wired to enforcement. strictness.ts was imported by exactly two non-test files — index.ts for a status readout and orion-authority for documentation — and validator.ts had never seen a mode. So `orion-mode contained` reported 'everything else asks first' and changed nothing that runs, and orion-incident freeze declined to drop the permission profile on the stated grounds that 'contained already stops every write'. That premise was false.

SERIOUS: a live credential was inside the backup. exec-approvals.json is staged and contains socket.token, 32 characters. Both exclusion layers matched filenames only, and the MANIFEST asserted 'No secret is in this archive'. The backup check never exercised the real sources() list — it planted a .env in its own fixture.

trusted_user is wider than 'Nick's own words'. hydrateFromTranscript mints it from any role:user line, and across 482 session files 496 such turns carry machine-authored prose. The orion-remote briefing — which opens 'Context from the transport, not from Nick' — contains the literal words 'yes, approve A-7F3K'. It did not approve anything, but only because exec matched the first occurrence, which sat in a non-affirmative clause. The guard was match ordering.
automation.ts used `p.action in AUTOMATION_ACTIONS`, which walks the prototype chain: constructor, toString, valueOf and __proto__ all passed a check whose job is to say the table is closed.
Phase 49's evidence said restoring the old hash acceptance fails four named assertions. It fails three.

orion-authority claimed the unclassified->APPROVAL rung means 'adding an allowlist entry cannot quietly grant silent execution'. With ask:off and askFallback:deny there is no ask state; it is a report, not a gate.

Phase 67's model counts and Phase 50's ladder numbers were pinned and are stale; Phase 52 cited askFallback in the wrong file; the Phase 76 alarm scans the installed dist rather than source, so an undeployed arrival is invisible.
reviews.verdict: Two findings with real safety cost, both repaired the same day with a named failing test for each. The gate's core claim — that the agent cannot satisfy its own approval — survived a direct attempt to break it.
